Semidefinite lower bounds for covering codes

Dion Gijswijt ††thanks: Delft Institute of Applied Mathematics, Delft University of Technology, The Netherlands. E-mail: d.c.gijswijt@tudelft.nl    Sven Polak ††thanks: Tilburg University, The Netherlands. E-mail: s.c.polak@tilburguniversity.edu
Abstract

Let Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) denote the minimum size of a qq-ary covering code of word length nn and covering radius rr. In other words, Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) is the minimum size of a set of qq-ary codewords of length nn such that the Hamming balls of radius rr around the codewords cover the Hamming space {0,…,q−1}n\{0,\ldots,q-1\}^{n}. The special case K3​(n,1)K_{3}(n,1) is often referred to as the football pool problem, as it is equivalent to finding a set of forecasts on nn football matches that is guaranteed to contain a forecast with at most one wrong outcome.

In this paper, we build and expand upon the work of Gijswijt (2005), who introduced a semidefinite programming lower bound on Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) via matrix cuts. We develop techniques that strengthen this bound, by introducing new semidefinite constraints inspired by Lasserre’s hierarchy for 0-1 programs and symmetry reduction methods, and a more powerful objective function. The techniques lead to sharper lower bounds, setting new records across a broad range of values of qq, nn, and rr.

1 Introduction

Let q≥2q\geq 2 and n≥1n\geq 1 be integers. Then [q]n:={0,…,q−1}n[q]^{n}:=\{0,\ldots,q-1\}^{n} is the Hamming space of qq-ary words of length nn. The Hamming distance between 𝐮,𝐯∈[q]n\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in[q]^{n} is denoted by d⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=|{i∈{1,…,n}:𝐮i≠𝐯i}|d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\mathbf{u}_{i}\neq\mathbf{v}_{i}\}|. We denote the isometry group of [q]n[q]^{n} by Aut⁡(q,n)\mathrm{Aut}(q,n). It consists of all permutations of [q]n[q]^{n} obtained by permuting the nn positions and independently permuting the qq symbols in each of the nn positions. The group Aut⁡(q,n)\mathrm{Aut}(q,n) acts on subsets S⊆[q]nS\subseteq[q]^{n}, vectors 𝐱∈ℂ[q]n\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{C}^{[q]^{n}} and matrices M∈ℂ[q]n×[q]nM\in\mathbb{C}^{[q]^{n}\times[q]^{n}} in the usual way by

σ​S={σ⁡(a)∣a∈S},(σ​𝐱)𝐮=𝐱σ−1​(𝐮),(σ​M)𝐮,𝐯=Mσ−1​(𝐮),σ−1​(𝐯)\sigma S=\{\sigma(a)\mid a\in S\},\quad(\sigma\mathbf{x})_{\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{x}_{\sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{u})},\quad(\sigma M)_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=M_{\sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{u}),\sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{v})}

for all σ∈Aut⁡(q,n)\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(q,n) and 𝐮,𝐯∈[q]n\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in[q]^{n}. For any integer 0≤r≤n0\leq r\leq n and any 𝐮∈[q]n\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n}, we denote by

Br​(𝐮)\displaystyle B_{r}(\mathbf{u}) :={𝐯∈[q]n∣d(𝐮,𝐯)≤r}and\displaystyle:=\{\mathbf{v}\in[q]^{n}\mid d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\leq r\}\quad\text{and}
Sr​(𝐮)\displaystyle S_{r}(\mathbf{u}) :={𝐯∈[q]n∣d⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=r}\displaystyle:=\{\mathbf{v}\in[q]^{n}\mid d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=r\}

the Hamming ball and Hamming sphere of radius rr around 𝐮\mathbf{u}, respectively.

A qq-ary code of length nn is a subset CC of [q]n[q]^{n}. The covering radius of CC is the smallest integer rr such that the Hamming balls of radius rr around the codewords cover the Hamming space [q]n[q]^{n}, i.e., ⋃𝐮∈CBr​(𝐮)=[q]n\bigcup_{\mathbf{u}\in C}B_{r}(\mathbf{u})=[q]^{n}. In this paper, we study the quantity

Kq​(n,r):=min​{|C|∣C⊆[q]n​ has covering radius r}.\displaystyle K_{q}(n,r):=\text{min}\{|C|\,\mid\,C\subseteq[q]^{n}\text{ has covering radius\penalty\ $r$}\}. (1)

In other words, the problem of determining Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) amounts to finding the smallest number of Hamming balls of radius rr that cover the Hamming space [q]n[q]^{n}. If C⊆[q]nC\subseteq[q]^{n} has covering radius rr and size K=|C|K=|C|, then we call CC an (n,K,q,r)(n,K,q,r)-code.

A popular application of covering codes is found in football pools. A football pool involves predicting the outcomes of nn football matches, where each match can result in three possible outcomes: a home team win, a draw, or an away team win. The objective is to find the smallest set of bets that is guaranteed to contain a bet with at most one incorrect outcome. This challenge, commonly known as the football pool problem, corresponds to the covering problem for q=3q=3 and r=1r=1. For more details on the football pool problem, see [8]. For an overview of results on covering codes and several of their applications, see [1].

A fundamental problem in the study of covering codes is to determine tight bounds on Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r). Upper bounds are commonly established by constructing an explicit code with covering radius rr. In this paper, we focus on establishing lower bounds on Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r).

Method of linear inequalities

A key approach for deriving lower bounds on Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) is the method of linear inequalities. Here, we follow the exposition in [1, Chapter 6]. Suppose we have a code C⊆[q]nC\subseteq[q]^{n} and define

Ai​(𝐮):=|C∩Si​(𝐮)|A_{i}(\mathbf{u}):=|C\cap S_{i}(\mathbf{u})|

for any 𝐮∈[q]n\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n} and i=0,…,ni=0,\ldots,n. The method considers valid linear inequalities over a code that are of the form

∑i=0nλi​Ai​(𝐮)≥βfor all ​𝐮∈[q]n,\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}A_{i}(\mathbf{u})\geq\beta\quad\text{for all }\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n}, (2)

where λ0,…,λn≥0\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n}\geq 0 and β>0\beta>0. Such a set of inequalities is denoted by (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta. The following proposition shows how such a set leads to a lower bound on Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r).

Proposition 1.1.

If every (n,K,q,r)(n,K,q,r)-code satisfies the inequalities (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta, then

K≥β​qn∑i=0nλi​(ni)​(q−1)i.K\geq\frac{\beta q^{n}}{\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}\binom{n}{i}(q-1)^{i}}.
Proof.

By summing the inequalities in (2) over all 𝐮∈[q]n\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n}, we obtain

β​qn≤∑𝐮∈[q]n∑i=0nλi​Ai​(𝐮)\displaystyle\beta q^{n}\leq\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n}}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}A_{i}(\mathbf{u}) =∑i=0nλi​∑𝐮∈[q]nAi​(𝐮)=∑i=0nλi​∑𝐯∈C|Si​(𝐯)|=|C|​∑i=0nλi​(ni)​(q−1)i.∎\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n}}A_{i}(\mathbf{u})=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}\sum_{\mathbf{v}\in C}|S_{i}(\mathbf{v})|=|C|\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}\tbinom{n}{i}(q-1)^{i}.\qed

The sphere covering inequalities of the form

∑i=0rAi​(𝐮)≥1for all ​𝐮∈[q]n\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{r}A_{i}(\mathbf{u})\geq 1\quad\text{for all }\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n} (3)

in combination with Proposition 1.1 lead to the sphere covering bound, given by

Kq​(n,r)≥qn∑i=0r(ni)​(q−1)i.\displaystyle K_{q}(n,r)\geq\frac{q^{n}}{\sum_{i=0}^{r}\tbinom{n}{i}(q-1)^{i}}. (4)

Several additional valid inequalities have been derived in the literature, especially in the binary case (q=2q=2), by analyzing how elements of Bs​(𝐮)B_{s}(\mathbf{u}) can be covered for s=1,2,3s=1,2,3. For s=1s=1, this results in the Van Wee inequalities [20, 21], given by:

∑i=0r−1⌈n+1r+1⌉​Ai​(𝐮)+Ar​(𝐮)+Ar+1​(𝐮)≥⌈n+1r+1⌉\displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}\left\lceil\frac{n+1}{r+1}\right\rceil A_{i}(\mathbf{u})+A_{r}(\mathbf{u})+A_{r+1}(\mathbf{u})\geq\left\lceil\frac{n+1}{r+1}\right\rceil (5)

which gives an improvement over the sphere covering bound when r+1r+1 does not divide n+1n+1. Additional inequalities can be found in articles by Johnson [9], Zhang [23], and Zhang and Lo [24].

By taking nonnegative linear combinations of inequalities, for instance by summing over sets Si​(𝐮)S_{i}(\mathbf{u}), new inequalities can be derived. Utilizing the fact that the Ai​(𝐮)A_{i}(\mathbf{u}) are integers, (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta implies (⌈λ0⌉,…,⌈λn⌉)​⌈β⌉(\lceil\lambda_{0}\rceil,\ldots,\lceil\lambda_{n}\rceil)\lceil\beta\rceil. This way, strengthened bounds can be found. For instance, the van Wee inequalities can be deduced from the sphere covering inequalities by summing over B1​(𝐮)B_{1}(\mathbf{u}), multiplying by 1r+1\tfrac{1}{r+1} and rounding up. Habsieger and Plagne extended this method to generate numerous new lower bounds for binary and ternary covering codes [7].

Semidefinite programming bounds

In [4, Section 5.3.1] a linear programming lower bound for Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) is given that is analogous to the Delsarte bound for error correcting codes [2].

If every code C⊆[q]nC\subseteq[q]^{n} with covering radius rr satisfies the inequalities (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta, then

Kq​(n,r)≥minx⁡qn​x0,K_{q}(n,r)\geq\min_{x}q^{n}x_{0},

where the minimum ranges over all nonnegative vectors x=(x0,x1,…,xn)𝖳∈ℝn+1x=(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})^{\sf T}\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1} that satisfy

  1. (i)

    ∑i=0nxi​Pk​(i)≥0\sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}P_{k}(i)\geq 0,

  2. (ii)

    ∑i=0nxi​∑j=0nλj​αi,jk≥β​x0\sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\lambda_{j}\alpha_{i,j}^{k}\geq\beta x_{0},

  3. (iii)

    ∑i=0n(x0−xi)​∑j=0nλj​αi,jk≥β⁡(1−x0)\sum_{i=0}^{n}(x_{0}-x_{i})\sum_{j=0}^{n}\lambda_{j}\alpha_{i,j}^{k}\geq\beta(1-x_{0}),

for all k=0,…,nk=0,\ldots,n. Here, Pk​(i):=∑s=0k(−1)s​(is)​(n−ik−s)​(q−1)k−sP_{k}(i):=\sum_{s=0}^{k}(-1)^{s}\tbinom{i}{s}\tbinom{n-i}{k-s}(q-1)^{k-s} are the Krawtchouk polynomials, and the numbers αi,jk\alpha_{i,j}^{k} are given by αi,jk=|{𝐯∈[q]n∣d(𝟎,𝐯)=i,d(𝐯,𝐮)=j}|\alpha_{i,j}^{k}=|\{\mathbf{v}\in[q]^{n}\mid d(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{v})=i,\,d(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u})=j\}| for any 𝐮∈[q]n\mathbf{u}\in[q]^{n} with d⁡(𝟎,𝐮)=kd(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{u})=k, and can be expressed as

αi,jk={∑p,tt+p=k+i−j(kt−p,p)​(n−ki−t)​(q−1)i−t​(q−2)t−pif ​q≥3,∑t2​t=k+i−j(kt)​(n−ki−t)if ​q=2.\alpha_{i,j}^{k}=\begin{cases}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}p,t\\ t+p=k+i-j\end{subarray}}\tbinom{k}{t-p,p}\tbinom{n-k}{i-t}(q-1)^{i-t}(q-2)^{t-p}&\text{if }q\geq 3,\\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\\ 2t=k+i-j\end{subarray}}\tbinom{k}{t}\tbinom{n-k}{i-t}&\text{if }q=2.\end{cases}

The n+1n+1 variables xix_{i} correspond to the distance distribution of the code. Where in the Delsarte bound variables corresponding to forbidden distances are set to zero, the bound on covering codes has inequalities (ii) and (iii) on the variables induced by the sphere covering inequalities, or any other valid set of inequalities (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta.

The Delsarte bound can be viewed as a semidefinite program where the [q]n×[q]n[q]^{n}\times[q]^{n} matrix variable is constrained to be invariant under Aut⁡(q,n)\mathrm{Aut}(q,n) (i.e., it is an element of the Bose-Mesner algebra of the Hamming scheme). Since the Bose-Mesner algebra has dimension n+1n+1, the matrix variable can be expressed in terms of n+1n+1 real variables (corresponding to the distance distribution of the code) and because the Bose-Mesner algebra is commutative, the semidefiniteness constraint can be reduced to linear constraints in the n+1n+1 variables by simultaneously diagonalizing the matrices in the Bose-Mesner algebra. This corresponds to inequalities (i).

For error correcting codes, strengthened SDP bounds based on the distribution of triples [19, 6] of codewords and four-tuples [5, 15] have been obtained. The main complication for these bounds is that the matrix variable is now an element of a non-commutative algebra. In the case of triple bounds, the relevant algebra consists of the [q]n×[q]n[q]^{n}\times[q]^{n} matrices that are invariant under Aut𝟎​(q,n)\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{0}}(q,n), the stabilizer subgroup with respect to the zero word. This algebra coincides with the Terwilliger algebra of the Hamming scheme. To reduce the SDP to an equivalent one of polynomial size, an explicit block diagonalization of this algebra had to be obtained.

An analogous bound for Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) based on triples of codewords, was obtained by Gijswijt in [4, Section 5.3.2] using the method of matrix cuts from [16]. Here, we develop techniques to strengthen this bound. We introduce new semidefinite constraints inspired by the Lasserre Hierarchy for 0-1 programs [12, 13] and symmetry reduction, alongside a more powerful objective function. The techniques lead to sharper lower bounds, improving the best known bounds for a broad range of values of qq, nn, and rr.

The bound we study in this paper is a covering analogue to Schrijver’s first SDP bounds for error-correcting codes in the finite Hamming space [19]. Such bounds can be interpreted as arising from submatrices corresponding to 3-point configurations in the second level of the Lasserre hierarchy [12] applied to a polynomial optimization formulation of the problem. In the context of discrete geometry and spherical codes, Riener, Rolfes, and Vallentin [18] recently proposed a hierarchy for spherical covering codes, inspired by hierarchies for packing problems in discrete geometry [11]. In our work, we extend Schrijver’s packing bound to covering codes in the finite Hamming space. While in principle one could also define a full hierarchy for covering codes in this setting, practical obstacles (in particular, the rapidly increasing number of variables and the size of the block matrices) make the full second and higher levels of the Lasserre hierarchy difficult to compute. Therefore, we focus on a 3-point bound and its symmetry reduction, and strengthen it as much as we can by introducing additional constraints and optimizing the choice of objective function.

Outline of the paper

In Section 2 we describe our SDP bound for covering codes in Theorem 2.5, before applying symmetry reduction. In Section 3 we describe the Terwilliger algebra of the binary and nonbinary Hamming schemes, which enables symmetry reduction of the bound from Section 2. In Section 4.1 we detail the symmetry reduction in the binary case (q=2q=2) and present the reduced bound in Theorem 4.9. Section 4.2 provides the reduced version of our SDP bound for the nonbinary case in Theorem 4.18. Finally, we present our improved bounds in tables in Section 5, with expanded versions of our numerical results in Appendices A and B.

Remark 2.1.

The conditions in Proposition 2.4 derive from general relaxations for 0-1 linear programs. In our setting, the incidence vector 𝐱∈{0,1}𝔼\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{E}} of CC satisfies the covering inequalities

∑i=0nλi​∑𝐯∈Si​(𝐮)𝐱𝐯≥βfor all 𝐮∈𝔼.\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}\sum_{\mathbf{v}\in S_{i}(\mathbf{u})}\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{v}}\geq\beta\quad\text{for all $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{E}$.}

However, the same method would apply in the setting of error correcting codes, where one might use inequalities 𝐱u+𝐱v≤1\mathbf{x}_{u}+\mathbf{x}_{v}\leq 1, if d⁡(𝐮,𝐯)∈{1,…,d−1}d(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\{1,\ldots,d-1\}.

The matrix NN and conditions (i)–(iii) come from the Lasserre Hierarchy for 0,10,1 polytopes. Let 𝐲\mathbf{y} be the extended incidence vector of CC, where for every subset S⊆𝔼S\subseteq\mathbb{E} we set 𝐲⁡(S)=1\mathbf{y}(S)=1 if S⊆CS\subseteq C and 𝐲⁡(S)=0\mathbf{y}(S)=0 otherwise. The validity of the covering inequalities implies that for every 𝐮∈𝔼\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{E}, the matrix M∈ℂ𝒫⁡(𝔼)×𝒫⁡(𝔼)M\in\mathbb{C}^{\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{E})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{E})} given by MI,J=∑i=0nλi​∑𝐯∈Si​(𝐮)yI∪J∪{𝐯}−β​yI∪JM_{I,J}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}\sum_{\mathbf{v}\in S_{i}(\mathbf{u})}y_{I\cup J\cup\{\mathbf{v}\}}-\beta y_{I\cup J} is positive semidefinite. Restricting to sets I,JI,J of size at most 11 and averaging over Aut⁡(q,n)\mathrm{Aut}(q,n) leads to the matrix NN and conditions (i)–(iii).

The four sets of inequalities in part (iv) come from matrix cut inequalities [16]. Let 𝐲∈ℂ∅∪𝔼\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{C}^{\emptyset\cup\mathbb{E}} be the extended incidence vector of CC where 𝐲∅=1\mathbf{y}_{\emptyset}=1, and 𝐲𝐮=1\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{u}}=1 if 𝐮∈C\mathbf{u}\in C and 𝐲𝐮=0\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{u}}=0 otherwise for 𝐮∈𝔼\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{E}. The vector 𝐱=𝐲\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y} satisfies the homogenized cover inequalities

∑i=0nλi​∑𝐯∈Si​(𝐮)𝐱𝐯≥β​𝐱∅for all 𝐮∈𝔼.\sum_{i=0}^{n}\lambda_{i}\sum_{\mathbf{v}\in S_{i}(\mathbf{u})}\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{v}}\geq\beta\mathbf{x}_{\emptyset}\quad\text{for all $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{E}$}. (8)

The positive semidefinite matrix 𝐲𝐲𝖳=R⁡(MC)\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^{\mathsf{T}}=R(M_{C}) has the property that every column satisfies (8), and so does the diagonal minus any column. Using the fact that for any σ∈Aut⁡(q,n)\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(q,n) also σ​C\sigma C has covering radius rr, and the fact that the sets of vectors 𝐱\mathbf{x} satisfying (8) is closed under nonnegative linear combinations, we thus obtain two sets of inequalities for (the bordered version of) the matrix M′M^{\prime}, and similarly for M′′M^{\prime\prime}. This yields the four conditions in (iv).

This leads to the following SDP lower bound on covering codes, which is always at least as tight as the LP bound mentioned in the introduction.11 1 The LP bound requires nonnegativity of certain expressions involving Krawtchouk polynomials, which is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of M=M′+M′′M=M^{\prime}+M^{\prime\prime}. The LP bound further requires that a small subset of the matrix cut inequalities are satisfied. Thus the LP constraints are implied by the SDP constraints of Theorem 2.5.

Theorem 2.5 (Covering lower bound).

Suppose that every C⊆𝔼C\subseteq\mathbb{E} with covering radius rr satisfies (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta. Then

Kq​(n,r)3≥minM,M′,M′′,N⁡qn​∑𝐮,𝐯∈𝔼M𝐮,𝐯′K_{q}(n,r)^{3}\geq\min_{M,M^{\prime},M^{\prime\prime},N}q^{n}\sum_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{E}}M^{\prime}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}

where the minimum ranges over real matrices M,M′,M′′,NM,M^{\prime},M^{\prime\prime},N that satisfy the conditions in Proposition 2.1, Proposition 2.2 and Proposition 2.4.

Remark 2.2.

The conditions in Proposition 2.1(i) and Proposition 2.4 express MM, M′′M^{\prime\prime} and NN in terms of M′M^{\prime}, so the minimization can be expressed in terms of the matrix variable M′M^{\prime} alone.

qn​∑𝐮,𝐯∈𝔼M𝐮,𝐯′3≥qn​∑𝐮∈𝔼M𝐮,𝐮′≥qn​M𝟎,𝟎′.\displaystyle\sqrt[3]{q^{n}\sum_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{E}}M^{\prime}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}}\geq\sqrt{q^{n}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{E}}M^{\prime}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}}}\geq q^{n}M^{\prime}_{\mathbf{0},\mathbf{0}}. (10)

⟨M′,J⟩2≥qn​⟨M′,I⟩3,implying(∑𝐮,𝐯∈𝔼M𝐮,𝐯′)2≥qn​(∑𝐮∈𝔼M𝐮,𝐮′)3.\langle M^{\prime},J\rangle^{2}\geq q^{n}\langle M^{\prime},I\rangle^{3},\quad\text{implying}\quad\big(\sum_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{E}}M^{\prime}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}\big)^{2}\geq q^{n}\big(\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{E}}M^{\prime}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{u}}\big)^{3}.

Multiplying both sides by q2​nq^{2n} and combining with (12) this yields (10), as desired.

In the next sections, we make the SDP from Theorem 2.5 effective by using symmetry reduction.

3 Block-diagonalization of the Terwilliger algebra

In this section, we describe the block-diagonalization of the Terwilliger algebras of the binary [19] and nonbinary [6] Hamming schemes. This forms the algebraic foundation for the symmetry reduction of the SDP in Theorem 2.5.

3.1 Terwilliger algebra of the binary Hamming cube

For 𝐮,𝐯∈{0,1}n\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\{0,1\}^{n} we define d¯​(𝐮,𝐯):=(i,j,t)\overline{d}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}):=(i,j,t), where

i\displaystyle i =|{ℓ∣𝐮ℓ≠0}|,\displaystyle=|\{\ell\mid\mathbf{u}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|,
j\displaystyle j =|{ℓ∣𝐯ℓ≠0}|,\displaystyle=|\{\ell\mid\mathbf{v}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|,
t\displaystyle t =|{ℓ∣𝐮ℓ≠0,𝐯ℓ≠0}|.\displaystyle=|\{\ell\mid\mathbf{u}_{\ell}\neq 0,\mathbf{v}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|.

The set of tuples (i,j,t)(i,j,t) that occur this way are given by

I(2,n)={(i,j,t)∣0≤t≤i,j,i+j≤n+t}I(2,n)=\{(i,j,t)\mid 0\leq t\leq i,j,\ i+j\leq n+t\}

and they parametrize the orbits of pairs (𝐮,𝐯)(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) under the group Aut𝟎​(2,n)={σ∈Aut⁡(2,n)∣σ⁡(𝟎)=𝟎}\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{0}}(2,n)=\{\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(2,n)\mid\sigma(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}\} of symmetries of the Hamming space that stabilize the zero word.

For (i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)(i,j,t)\in I(2,n) we define the {0,1}n×{0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{n} matrix Mi,jtM_{i,j}^{t} by

(Mi,jt)𝐮,𝐯={1if ​d¯​(𝐮,𝐯)=(i,j,t)0otherwise.\left(M_{i,j}^{t}\right)_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\overline{d}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=(i,j,t)\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

The matrices Mi,jtM_{i,j}^{t} constitute a basis for the space 𝒜2,n\mathcal{A}_{2,n} of complex {0,1}n×{0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}\times\{0,1\}^{n} matrices that are invariant under the action of Aut𝟎​(2,n)\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{0}}(2,n):

𝒜2,n={∑(i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)xi,jt​Mi,jt∣xi,jt∈ℂ}.\mathcal{A}_{2,n}=\left\{\sum_{(i,j,t)\in I(2,n)}x_{i,j}^{t}M_{i,j}^{t}\mid x_{i,j}^{t}\in\mathbb{C}\right\}.

Note that (Mi,jt)𝖳=Mj,it(M_{i,j}^{t})^{\sf T}=M_{j,i}^{t}. Moreover, if |supp(𝐮)|=i|\supp(\mathbf{u})|=i, |supp(𝐯)|=j|\supp(\mathbf{v})|=j, then |supp(𝐮)∩supp(𝐯)|=t|\supp(\mathbf{u})\cap\supp(\mathbf{v})|=t is equivalent to dH​(𝐮,𝐯)=i+j−2​td_{H}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=i+j-2t. The set 𝒜2,n\mathcal{A}_{2,n} is a C∗C^{*}-algebra, i.e., it is closed under taking the adjoint, addition, scalar multiplication, and matrix multiplication. This algebra is the Terwilliger algebra of the binary Hamming scheme. We will now describe the block diagonalization of this algebra, which was derived by Schrijver [19], and which allows a significant reduction in the size of matrices of 𝒜2,n\mathcal{A}_{2,n} by mapping it to an isomorphic smaller algebra. To this end, define, for i,j,k,t∈{0,…,n}i,j,k,t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}, the numbers

βi,j,kt=∑u=0n(−1)t−u​(ut)​(n−2​ku−k)​(n−k−ui−u)​(n−k−uj−u).\displaystyle\beta_{i,j,k}^{t}=\sum_{u=0}^{n}(-1)^{t-u}\tbinom{u}{t}\tbinom{n-2k}{u-k}\tbinom{n-k-u}{i-u}\tbinom{n-k-u}{j-u}. (13)

Throughout the paper, we use the convention that (st)=0\tbinom{s}{t}=0 if s<ts<t or t<0t<0.

Theorem 3.1.

[19] The following map is a ∗*-isomorphism of algebras:

ϕ:𝒜2,n\displaystyle\phi:\mathcal{A}_{2,n} →⨁k=0⌊n/2⌋ℂn−2​k+1×n−2​k+1\displaystyle\to\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\mathbb{C}^{n-2k+1\times n-2k+1}
∑(i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)xi,jt​Mi,jt\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j,t)\in I(2,n)}x_{i,j}^{t}M_{i,j}^{t} ↦⨁k=0⌊n/2⌋(∑t(n−2​ki−k)−12​(n−2​kj−k)−12​βi,j,kt​xi,jt)i,j=kn−k.\displaystyle\mapsto\bigoplus_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\left(\sum_{t}\tbinom{n-2k}{i-k}^{-\tfrac{1}{2}}\tbinom{n-2k}{j-k}^{-\tfrac{1}{2}}\beta_{i,j,k}^{t}x_{i,j}^{t}\right)_{i,j=k}^{n-k}. (14)

Theorem 3.1 implies that, for coefficients xi,jt∈ℂx_{i,j}^{t}\in\mathbb{C}, we have

∑(i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)xi,jtMi,jt⪰0⟺(∑tβi,j,ktxi,jt)i,j=kn−k⪰0 for all k=0,…,⌊n/2⌋.\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j,t)\in I(2,n)}x_{i,j}^{t}M_{i,j}^{t}\succeq 0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\left(\sum_{t}\beta_{i,j,k}^{t}x_{i,j}^{t}\right)_{i,j=k}^{n-k}\succeq 0\text{ for all $k=0,\ldots,{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$.} (15)

3.2 Terwilliger algebra of the nonbinary Hamming scheme

For 𝐮,𝐯∈[q]n\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in[q]^{n} we define d¯​(𝐮,𝐯):=(i,j,t,p)\overline{d}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}):=(i,j,t,p) where

i\displaystyle i =|{ℓ∣𝐮ℓ≠0}|,\displaystyle=|\{\ell\mid\mathbf{u}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|,
j\displaystyle j =|{ℓ∣𝐯ℓ≠0}|,\displaystyle=|\{\ell\mid\mathbf{v}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|,
t\displaystyle t =|{ℓ∣𝐮ℓ≠0,𝐯ℓ≠0}|,\displaystyle=|\{\ell\mid\mathbf{u}_{\ell}\neq 0,\mathbf{v}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|,
p\displaystyle p =|{ℓ∣𝐮ℓ=𝐯ℓ≠0}|.\displaystyle=|\{\ell\mid\mathbf{u}_{\ell}=\mathbf{v}_{\ell}\neq 0\}|.

The set of tuples (i,j,t,p)(i,j,t,p) that occur this way are given by

I(q,n)={(i,j,t,p)∣0≤p≤t≤i,j,i+j≤n+t}I(q,n)=\{(i,j,t,p)\mid 0\leq p\leq t\leq i,j,\ i+j\leq n+t\}

and they parametrize the orbits of pairs (𝐮,𝐯)(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) under the group Aut𝟎​(q,n)={σ∈Aut⁡(q,n)∣σ⁡(𝟎)=𝟎}\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{0}}(q,n)=\{\sigma\in\mathrm{Aut}(q,n)\mid\sigma(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}\} of symmetries of the Hamming space that stabilize the zero word.

For (i,j,t,p)∈I⁡(q,n)(i,j,t,p)\in I(q,n) we define the [q]n×[q]n[q]^{n}\times[q]^{n} matrix Mi,jt,pM_{i,j}^{t,p} by

(Mi,jt,p)𝐮,𝐯={1if ​d¯​(𝐮,𝐯)=(i,j,t,p)0otherwise.\left(M_{i,j}^{t,p}\right)_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\overline{d}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=(i,j,t,p)\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

The matrices Mi,jt,pM_{i,j}^{t,p} constitute a basis for the space 𝒜q,n\mathcal{A}_{q,n} of complex [q]n×[q]n[q]^{n}\times[q]^{n} matrices that are invariant under the action of Aut𝟎​(q,n)\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{0}}(q,n):

𝒜q,n={∑(i,j,t,p)∈I⁡(q,n)xi,jt,p​Mi,jt,p∣xi,jt,p∈ℂ}.\mathcal{A}_{q,n}=\left\{\sum_{(i,j,t,p)\in I(q,n)}x_{i,j}^{t,p}M_{i,j}^{t,p}\mid x_{i,j}^{t,p}\in\mathbb{C}\right\}.

This space is a C∗C^{*}-algebra and coincides with the Terwilliger algebra of the nonbinary Hamming scheme. An explicit block diagonalisation of 𝒜q,n\mathcal{A}_{q,n} was given in [6]. To describe it, define for any nonnegative integers i,j,t,p,a,ki,j,t,p,a,k the number

α⁡(i,j,t,p,a,k)=βi−a,j−a,k−an−a,t−a⋅(q−1)12​(i+j)−t⋅∑g=0p(−1)a−g​(ag)​(t−ap−g)​(q−2)t−a−p+g.\alpha(i,j,t,p,a,k)=\beta^{n-a,t-a}_{i-a,j-a,k-a}\cdot(q-1)^{\tfrac{1}{2}(i+j)-t}\cdot\sum_{g=0}^{p}(-1)^{a-g}\tbinom{a}{g}\tbinom{t-a}{p-g}(q-2)^{t-a-p+g}.
Theorem 3.4 ([6]).

The following map is a ∗*-isomorphism of algebras:

ϕ:𝒜q,n\displaystyle\phi:\mathcal{A}_{q,n} →⨁0≤a≤k≤n+a−kℂ(n+a−2​k+1)×(n+a−2​k+1)\displaystyle\to\bigoplus_{0\leq a\leq k\leq n+a-k}\mathbb{C}^{(n+a-2k+1)\times(n+a-2k+1)}
∑(i,j,t,p)xi,jt,p​Mi,jt,p\displaystyle\sum_{(i,j,t,p)}x_{i,j}^{t,p}M_{i,j}^{t,p} ↦⨁0≤a≤k≤n+a−k(∑t,p(n+a−2​ki−k)−12​(n+a−2​kj−k)−12​α​(i,j,t,p,a,k)​xi,jt,p)i,j=kn+a−k.\displaystyle\mapsto\bigoplus_{0\leq a\leq k\leq n+a-k}\left(\sum_{t,p}\tbinom{n+a-2k}{i-k}^{-\tfrac{1}{2}}\tbinom{n+a-2k}{j-k}^{-\tfrac{1}{2}}\alpha(i,j,t,p,a,k)x_{i,j}^{t,p}\right)_{i,j=k}^{n+a-k}. (18)

This theorem implies that a matrix M∈𝒜q,nM\in\mathcal{A}_{q,n} is positive semidefinite if and only if ϕ⁡(A)\phi(A) is positive semidefinite. We also note that for real valued matrices AA, the image ϕ⁡(A)\phi(A) is again real. To see the size of the reduction, note that the matrices in 𝒜q,n\mathcal{A}_{q,n} have size qn×qnq^{n}\times q^{n}, while for q≥3q\geq 3 we have (cf. [6])

|I⁡(q,n)|=∑0≤a≤k≤n+a−k(n+a−2​k+1)2=(n+44),\displaystyle|I(q,n)|=\sum_{0\leq a\leq k\leq n+a-k}(n+a-2k+1)^{2}=\binom{n+4}{4}, (19)

which equals the dimension of 𝒜q,n\mathcal{A}_{q,n}.

As in the binary case, we need to deal with bordered matrices R⁡(M)R(M) for M∈𝒜q,nM\in\mathcal{A}_{q,n}. To express semidefiniteness of R⁡(M)R(M) in terms of ϕ⁡(M)\phi(M), we need the following two lemmas22 2 Analogous to the binary case (see Remark 3.1), Lemma 3.6 can also be derived directly from the explicit block diagonalisation given in [6]..

Lemma 3.5.

We have

∑p,tα⁡(i,j,t,p,a,k)={(ni)​(nj)​(q−1)12​(i+j)if a=k=00otherwise.\sum_{p,t}\alpha(i,j,t,p,a,k)=\begin{cases}\tbinom{n}{i}\tbinom{n}{j}(q-1)^{\tfrac{1}{2}(i+j)}&\text{if $a=k=0$}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

=∑g≥0(−1)a−g​(ag)⋅∑s≥0(t−as)​(q−2)t−a−s.\displaystyle=\sum_{g\geq 0}(-1)^{a-g}\tbinom{a}{g}\cdot\sum_{s\geq 0}\tbinom{t-a}{s}(q-2)^{t-a-s}.

∑t,pα⁡(i,j,t,p,0,k)=(q−1)12​(i+j)​∑tβi,j,kt=(q−1)12​(i+j)​(ni)​(nj)​δk,0.\sum_{t,p}\alpha(i,j,t,p,0,k)=(q-1)^{\tfrac{1}{2}(i+j)}\sum_{t}\beta_{i,j,k}^{t}=(q-1)^{\tfrac{1}{2}(i+j)}\tbinom{n}{i}\tbinom{n}{j}\delta_{k,0}.

Similar to the binary case, we have

Let M=∑(i,j,t,p)∈I⁡(q,n)xi,jt,p​Mi,jt,p∈𝒜q,nM=\sum_{(i,j,t,p)\in I(q,n)}x_{i,j}^{t,p}M_{i,j}^{t,p}\in\mathcal{A}_{q,n} and let

4 The symmetry-reduced SDP bound

In this section we demonstrate how the block-diagonalization from the Terwilliger algebra as described in Section 3 can be employed to significantly reduce the new SDP bound for covering codes from Section 2.

4.1 The SDP bound for binary covering codes

In the binary case, the matrices M′M^{\prime}, M′′M^{\prime\prime} and NN from Section 2 are contained in the algebra 𝒜2,n\mathcal{A}_{2,n}. So we can write

M′=∑(i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)xi,jt​Mi,jt\displaystyle M^{\prime}=\sum_{(i,j,t)\in I(2,n)}x_{i,j}^{t}M_{i,j}^{t} (20)

for real numbers xi,jtx_{i,j}^{t}.

Lemma 4.1.

We have

M=∑(i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)xi+j−2​t,00​Mi,jt,M′′=∑(i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)(xi+j−2​t,00−xi,jt)​Mi,jt.M=\sum_{(i,j,t)\in I(2,n)}x_{i+j-2t,0}^{0}M_{i,j}^{t},\qquad M^{\prime\prime}=\sum_{(i,j,t)\in I(2,n)}(x_{i+j-2t,0}^{0}-x_{i,j}^{t})M_{i,j}^{t}.
Proof.

Note that if 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔼\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{E} with d¯​(𝐮,𝐯)=(i,j,t)\overline{d}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=(i,j,t), then d⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=i+j−2​td(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=i+j-2t. So M𝐮,𝐯=xi+j−2​t,00M_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=x_{i+j-2t,0}^{0} and M𝐮,𝐯′′=xi+j−2​t,00−xi,jtM^{\prime\prime}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=x_{i+j-2t,0}^{0}-x_{i,j}^{t} by Proposition 2.1 (i). ∎

Remark 4.1 (Interpretation of the xi,jtx_{i,j}^{t}).

The coefficients xi,jtx_{i,j}^{t} provide insight into the structure of the code CC by extending the concept of distance distribution in Delsarte’s linear programming approach to triples. Whereas the distance distribution tracks the number of pairs in CC at each distance dd, the coefficients xi,jtx_{i,j}^{t} count the number of triples (𝐮,𝐯,𝐰)∈C3(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})\in C^{3} that belong to an equivalence class of 𝔼3\mathbb{E}^{3} under the group action of Aut​(2,n)\text{Aut}(2,n). We proceed by explaining this formally. Define

Xi,j,t:={(𝐮,𝐯,𝐰)∈𝔼×𝔼×𝔼∣d¯​(𝐯−𝐮,𝐰−𝐮)=(i,j,t)},X_{i,j,t}:=\{(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})\in\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E}\mid\overline{d}(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{u})=(i,j,t)\},

for (i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)(i,j,t)\in I(2,n). For each (i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)(i,j,t)\in I(2,n), define the numbers

λi,jt:=|(C×C×C)∩Xi,j,t|,\lambda_{i,j}^{t}:=|(C\times C\times C)\cap X_{i,j,t}|,

and let

γi,jt:=|({𝟎}×𝔼×𝔼)∩Xi,j,t|=(ni−t,j−t,t)\gamma_{i,j}^{t}:=|(\{\mathbf{0}\}\times\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E})\cap X_{i,j,t}|=\binom{n}{i-t,j-t,t}

be the number of nonzero entries of Mi,jtM_{i,j}^{t}. Then the coefficients xi,jtx_{i,j}^{t} are given by

xi,jt=2−n​(γi,jt)−1​λi,jt.\displaystyle x_{i,j}^{t}=2^{-n}(\gamma_{i,j}^{t})^{-1}\lambda_{i,j}^{t}. (21)

To see (21), notice that the matrices Mi,jtM_{i,j}^{t} are pairwise orthogonal, and their inner products satisfy ⟨Mi,jt,Mi,jt⟩=γi,jt\langle M_{i,j}^{t},M_{i,j}^{t}\rangle=\gamma_{i,j}^{t}, for (i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)(i,j,t)\in I(2,n). Thus, we compute:

⟨M′,Mi,jt⟩\displaystyle\langle M^{\prime},M_{i,j}^{t}\rangle =|Aut​(2,n)|−1​∑𝐮∈C∑σ∈Aut​(2,n)σ​𝐮=𝟎⟨Mσ​C,Mi,jt⟩\displaystyle=|\text{Aut}(2,n)|^{-1}\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in C}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\text{Aut}(2,n)\\ \sigma\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}\end{subarray}}\langle M_{\sigma C},M_{i,j}^{t}\rangle
=|Aut(2,n)|−1⋅|Aut𝟎(2,n)|∑𝐮∈C|({𝐮}×C×C)∩Xi,j,t|\displaystyle=|\text{Aut}(2,n)|^{-1}\cdot|\text{Aut}_{\mathbf{0}}(2,n)|\sum_{\mathbf{u}\in C}|(\{\mathbf{u}\}\times C\times C)\cap X_{i,j,t}|
=2−n​|(C×C×C)∩Xi,j,t|=2−n​λi,jt.\displaystyle=2^{-n}|(C\times C\times C)\cap X_{i,j,t}|=2^{-n}\lambda_{i,j}^{t}.

Hence we have

M′=2−n​∑(i,j,t)∈I⁡(2,n)λi,jt​(γi,jt)−1​Mi,jt.M^{\prime}=2^{-n}\sum_{(i,j,t)\in I(2,n)}\lambda_{i,j}^{t}(\gamma_{i,j}^{t})^{-1}M_{i,j}^{t}.

Comparing the coefficients of each Mi,jtM_{i,j}^{t} in this expression with those in (20) establishes (21).

Proposition 4.2 (Basic inequalities and symmetry).

The xi,jtx_{i,j}^{t} satisfy

(i) 0≤xi,jt≤xi,ii,\displaystyle\quad\quad 0\leq x_{i,j}^{t}\leq x_{i,i}^{i}, (22)
(ii) xi,00+xi+j−2​t,00−x0,00≤xi,jt≤xi+j−2​t,00,\displaystyle\quad\quad x_{i,0}^{0}+x^{0}_{i+j-2t,0}-x_{0,0}^{0}\leq x_{i,j}^{t}\leq x^{0}_{i+j-2t,0},
(iii) xi,jt=xi′,j′t′​ if (i,j,i+j−2​t) is a permutation of (i′,j′,i′+j′−2​t′),\displaystyle\quad\quad x_{i,j}^{t}=x_{i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}^{t^{\prime}}\,\,\,\text{ if $(i,j,i+j-2t)$ is a permutation of $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}-2t^{\prime})$},
Proof.

This follows directly from Proposition 2.1 (ii), (iii), (iv) combined with Lemma 4.1. ∎

Theorem 4.9.

If every code C⊆𝔼C\subseteq\mathbb{E} with covering radius rr satisfies (λ0,λ1,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta, then we have

By (16), both the number of variables of the reduced SDP and the sum of squares of its block sizes are O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}).

4.2 The SDP bound for nonbinary covering codes

In this section, we address the nonbinary case, that is, q≥3q\geq 3. The overall strategy is the same as in the binary case discussed in the previous section, so the arguments are analogous. However, the formulas involve additional terms and variables, making them more cumbersome to write out explicitly. To avoid redundancy, we keep proofs brief.

The matrices M′M^{\prime}, M′′M^{\prime\prime} and NN from Section 2 are contained in the algebra 𝒜q,n\mathcal{A}_{q,n}. So we can write

M′=∑(i,j,t,p)∈I⁡(q,n)xi,jt,p​Mi,jt,p\displaystyle M^{\prime}=\sum_{(i,j,t,p)\in I(q,n)}x_{i,j}^{t,p}M_{i,j}^{t,p} (31)

for real numbers xi,jt,px_{i,j}^{t,p}.

Lemma 4.10.

We have

M=∑i,j,t,pxi+j−t−p,00,0​Mi,jt,p,M′′=∑i,j,t,p(xi+j−t−p,00,0−xi,jt,p)​Mi,jt,p.M=\sum_{i,j,t,p}x_{i+j-t-p,0}^{0,0}M_{i,j}^{t,p},\qquad M^{\prime\prime}=\sum_{i,j,t,p}(x_{i+j-t-p,0}^{0,0}-x_{i,j}^{t,p})M_{i,j}^{t,p}.
Proof.

Note that if 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔼\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{E} with d¯​(𝐮,𝐯)=(i,j,t,p)\overline{d}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=(i,j,t,p), then d⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=i+j−t−pd(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=i+j-t-p. So M𝐮,𝐯=xi+j−t−p,00,0M_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=x_{i+j-t-p,0}^{0,0} and M𝐮,𝐯′′=xi+j−t−p,00,0−xi,jt,pM^{\prime\prime}_{\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}}=x_{i+j-t-p,0}^{0,0}-x_{i,j}^{t,p} by Proposition 2.1 (i). ∎

Remark 4.2 (Interpretation of the xi,jt,px_{i,j}^{t,p}).

Similar to the binary case, the coefficients xi,jt,px_{i,j}^{t,p} provide insight into the structure of the code CC by extending the concept of distance distribution in Delsarte’s linear programming approach to triples. The xi,jt,px_{i,j}^{t,p} count the number of triples (𝐮,𝐯,𝐰)∈C3(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})\in C^{3} that belong to an equivalence class of 𝔼3\mathbb{E}^{3} under the group action of Aut​(q,n)\text{Aut}(q,n). Define

Xi,j,t,p:={(𝐮,𝐯,𝐰)∈𝔼×𝔼×𝔼∣d¯​(𝐯−𝐮,𝐰−𝐮)=(i,j,t,p)},X_{i,j,t,p}:=\{(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w})\in\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E}\mid\overline{d}(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{u})=(i,j,t,p)\},

for (i,j,t,p)∈I⁡(q,n)(i,j,t,p)\in I(q,n). For each (i,j,t,p)∈I⁡(q,n)(i,j,t,p)\in I(q,n), define the numbers

λi,jt,p:=|(C×C×C)∩Xi,j,t,p|,\lambda_{i,j}^{t,p}:=|(C\times C\times C)\cap X_{i,j,t,p}|,

and let

γi,jt,p:=|({𝟎}×𝔼×𝔼)∩Xi,j,t,p|=(q−1)i+j−t​(q−2)t−p​(np,t−p,i−t,j−t)\gamma_{i,j}^{t,p}:=|(\{\mathbf{0}\}\times\mathbb{E}\times\mathbb{E})\cap X_{i,j,t,p}|=(q-1)^{i+j-t}(q-2)^{t-p}\binom{n}{p,t-p,i-t,j-t}

be the number of nonzero entries of Mi,jt,pM_{i,j}^{t,p}. Then the coefficients xi,jt,px_{i,j}^{t,p} are given by

xi,jt,p=q−n​(γi,jt,p)−1​λi,jt,p.\displaystyle x_{i,j}^{t,p}=q^{-n}(\gamma_{i,j}^{t,p})^{-1}\lambda_{i,j}^{t,p}. (32)

Equation (32) can be seen with an analogous computation as was done to show (21) for the binary case. To prevent repetition, we omit the details.

and t−p=t′−p′,\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\text{and $t-p=t^{\prime}-p^{\prime}$},

This follows directly from Proposition 2.1 (ii), (iii), (iv) combined with Lemma 4.10. ∎

The following theorem makes the semidefinite programming lower bound from Theorem 2.5 effective using symmetry reduction for general qq-ary codes, that is, it gives an efficient semidefinite programming lower bound on Kq​(n,r)K_{q}(n,r) for arbitrary qq.

Theorem 4.18.

If every code C⊆𝔼C\subseteq\mathbb{E} with covering radius rr satisfies (λ0,λ1,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta, then we have

Kq​(n,r)3≥minx⁡qn​∑(i,j,t,p)∈I⁡(q,n)(q−1)i+j−t​(q−2)t−p​(np,t−p,i−t,j−t)​xi,jt,p,\displaystyle K_{q}(n,r)^{3}\geq\min_{x}q^{n}\sum_{(i,j,t,p)\in I(q,n)}(q-1)^{i+j-t}(q-2)^{t-p}\binom{n}{p,t-p,i-t,j-t}x_{i,j}^{t,p}, (44)

where the minimum ranges over all real x=(xi,jt,p)x=(x_{i,j}^{t,p}) satisfying the constraints from Propositions 4.11, 4.12, 4.14, and 4.17.

Proof.

Equation (44) is the objective function from Theorem 2.5 written in terms of the xi,jt,px_{i,j}^{t,p}. The validity of the constraints from Propositions 4.11, 4.12, 4.14, and 4.17 was already proven. ∎

By (19), both the number of variables of the reduced SDP and the sum of squares of its block sizes are O⁡(n4)O(n^{4}).

5 Tables with the new lower bounds

We used Julia to generate the semidefinite programs. We also developed an independent Perl code to generate the SDPs, which we used to validate our Julia code. Most SDPs were solved directly in Julia via JuMP with the high-precision solver SDPA-GMP [17]. The solving time varied from a few seconds to several days for the larger instances in the tables below. The precision in SDPA-GMP was set to 512 bits, and custom parameters (mainly a larger lambdaStar, the parameter which determines an initial point for the interior point method) were used as opposed to the standard parameter settings provided with SDPA-GMP to ensure convergence for the larger instances.

Generating the SDP for larger instances posed additional challenges due to large coefficients, necessitating the use of high-precision numbers (we used 512 bits BigFloats). Our code for generating the SDP including the call to the solver SDPA-GMP and the parameters used for most of the instances we solved, is available here:

https://github.com/CoveringCodes

In the following tables, we present our new bounds obtained from the semidefinite programs in Theorem 4.9 and 4.18, and compare them to the best known bounds from Keri’s tables [10]. While we also find improved bounds of K2​(18,1)≥14665K_{2}(18,1)\geq 14665 and K2​(30,1)≥35874398K_{2}(30,1)\geq 35874398, these have recently been surpassed by Wu and Chen [22], who established K2​(18,1)≥14666K_{2}(18,1)\geq 14666 and K2​(30,1)≥35876816K_{2}(30,1)\geq 35876816. Therefore we exclude these bounds from Table 1.

To illustrate the size of the computations, we report the number of variables in the final symmetry-reduced SDP, together with the sum of the block sizes in the block-diagonalization of M′M^{\prime} and the sum of the squares of these block sizes, see Table 4. We note that the dimensions of the Terwilliger algebras are (n+33)\tbinom{n+3}{3} in the binary case, and (n+44)\tbinom{n+4}{4} in the nonbinary case, but the actual number of variables in our SDP is smaller, since the additional symmetry relations from Propositions 4.2 (iii) and 4.11 (iii) are imposed.

By Theorems 3.1 and 3.4, the block sizes in the block diagonalization of M′M^{\prime} are given by n−2​k+1n-2k+1 for k=0,…,⌊n/2⌋k=0,\ldots,\lfloor n/2\rfloor in the binary case, and n+a−2​k+1n+a-2k+1 for all pairs (a,k)(a,k) with 0≤a≤k≤n+a−k0\leq a\leq k\leq n+a-k in the nonbinary case. The matrices M′′M^{\prime\prime} and NN have the same block structure after block-diagonalization, except that the block corresponding to k=0k=0 or (a,k)=(0,0)(a,k)=(0,0) is bordered, increasing its size by one. The table reports the block sizes after symmetry reduction for the matrix M′M^{\prime}. The full SDP contains several semidefinite constraints (for M′M^{\prime}, M′′M^{\prime\prime}, and one or more matrices NN), each with essentially the same block sizes. Thus, the total size of the SDP is a small constant multiple of the values reported in the table.

The computational effort also depends on the choice of inequalities (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta, since the construction of the entries of the matrices NN involves combinatorial sums whose number of terms increases with the number of nonzero coefficients λi\lambda_{i}. Consequently, for larger RR the SDP takes much longer to generate, and typically also to solve, even though the block sizes and the number of variables remain unchanged for fixed nn.

The total running time (including both SDP generation and solving) ranged from a few minutes for smaller instances to several days on standard desktop hardware, and in some cases up to two weeks for the largest instances. These runtimes depend strongly on the parameters (q,n,R)(q,n,R), the numerical precision, and solver settings. In particular, we used SDPA-GMP, as the SDPs can have very large coefficients and appear to require high-precision arithmetic for reliable solution. The reported runtimes should therefore be interpreted as indicative. All SDPs could very comfortably be generated and solved on a machine with 32 GB of RAM, although the generation and solving of larger instances required several gigabytes due to the use of high-precision arithmetic.

Appendix A All computational results for q=2q=2

We computed the lower bounds following from Theorem 4.9 using the two (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta coming from the sphere covering inequalities and the Van Wee inequalities. So positive semidefiniteness of the Lasserre matrices and the matrix cut inequalities for both (λ0,…,λn)​β(\lambda_{0},\ldots,\lambda_{n})\beta are included as constraints.
